strengths: This paper attempts to tackle an important problem which I agree has not been solved by existing DP literature.
The theoretical analysis is rigorous and thorough and I have limited criticisms if this is pitched primarily as a theory paper.
The writing of this paper is quite good. The paper was easy enough to follow, and the results were cleanly written.
Working in low-dimensions is an important theme for computational and sample efficiency, so their work makes sense in that regime.
They don't require the data to have large eigenvalue gaps, so it is general enough by itself.
The authors proposed a polynomial-time algorithm for DP synthetic data that can be more accurate than previous methods if the data is lying in a low dimensional subspace.
The value of $d'$ can be chosen adaptively by looking at the singular values of the privatized covariance matrix.
Privacy and utility analysis of the algorithm are provided.
The paper is fairly easy to understand, despite being theory-heavy.
Using PCA in this way to get around the curse of dimensionality in DP synthetic data generation is novel to my knowledge.
weaknesses: It is unclear how a practitioner looking to use this approach would know whether their data fits the regime in which the utility theorems hold, and the experiments are very limited, providing little information into the practical utility of the approach to most real‑world datasets; the experiments need to be extended to a much wider set of datasets and downstream tasks.

The baseline in Figure 2 is not appropriate; the authors should compare to training the classifier with DP‑SGD directly without creating synthetic data and to a classifier trained without DP, and include a broader set of tasks in the experiments.
The paper lacks further intuition and descriptions of the algorithms in surrounding text, making it less readable because it explains what each part does but not why it is a good idea.

The expected Wasserstein distance bound contains a third term that does not help when $d$ is large and $d'$ is not too small, creating a trade‑off where the second term becomes too large if $d'$ is large.
More empirical evaluation would have been nice for this venue; given the potential practical applications, additional experimental work would have made sense.
The empirical accuracy is not significant when $\varepsilon$ is small, even as small as 1, although it does better than a direct application of the work from He et al (2023).

The experimental comparison against the full‑dimension algorithm is convincing, but the authors should also compare against the method of Donhauser et al. (2023), especially since they claim higher accuracy.

There should be a discussion on the $\sqrt{\sum_{i>d'}\sigma_i(M)}$ term, especially when $d'$ is unknown; it is unclear how the algorithm would perform if the singular values decay slowly or there is no clear gap in the spectrum.
The reviewer is not fully convinced that the proposed method performs strictly better than that of Donhauser et al. (2023).

The Laplace mechanism should be introduced and its privacy guarantee stated; the parameter should be $\frac{\Delta_1}{\epsilon}$ with $\Delta_1$ as the $L_1$‑sensitivity, and the current use with $\Delta_1=\frac{1}{n}$ is incorrect for $d$‑dimensional data.
The private covariance matrix and private linear projection steps in Algorithm 1 should have $\epsilon/4$ rather than $\epsilon/2$, since the privacy budget must be split among four mechanisms.
The paper should explicitly state that image labels are considered public information in the experiments and thus have no privacy protection.

The generated images look very poor compared to those in the DP‑MERF paper (Harder et al. 2021) for MNIST; a comparison with DP‑MERF on the same dataset would provide a more meaningful assessment of practical value.
